title: Network Foundations

weeks.focus: Model and freeze the network path

evidence: Build review and Week 18 learning log
Evaluation, remediation, and Week 20 learning log

readiness_note: Ready on 2026-08-01 after structural and semantic review, 22 lab tests, six accepted isolated calibration runs, deterministic checking, focused and full course validation, and evidence-safety review.

outcomes.statement: Model a client journey as a layered path with round-trip, byte, bandwidth-delay-product, and tail-latency budgets.
Trace DNS resolution, addressing, routing, caching, and discovery with explicit authority, expiry, and failure boundaries.
Relate TCP ordering, loss recovery, flow control, congestion control, and receiver behavior to measured goodput and tail latency.
Trace TLS authentication and handshake costs while preserving hostname, certificate, key, resumption, and trust boundaries.
Diagnose proxy, load-balancer, NAT, connection-pool, and slow-reader behavior with capacity, ownership, and cost evidence.
Compare HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 through setup, multiplexing, stream isolation, fallback, observability, and client-network constraints.
Diagnose nine hidden network faults from preserved evidence before reveal and design reruns that separate credible causes.
Defend a protocol and topology decision through client outcomes, security, cost, ownership, migration, rollback, and reversal conditions.

challenge_questions.prompt: Which claim in your artifact most directly supports this outcome, and what evidence could falsify it: Model a client journey as a layered path with round-trip, byte, bandwidth-delay-product, and tail-latency budgets.

What unstated assumption could invalidate your treatment of this outcome, and how would you test it: Trace DNS resolution, addressing, routing, caching, and discovery with explicit authority, expiry, and failure boundaries.

Defend the causal chain behind your evidence for this outcome, including the first likely failure: Relate TCP ordering, loss recovery, flow control, congestion control, and receiver behavior to measured goodput and tail latency.

Which reasonable alternative would challenge your treatment of this outcome, and under what evidence would it win: Trace TLS authentication and handshake costs while preserving hostname, certificate, key, resumption, and trust boundaries.

What operational, security, cost, or ownership consequence is least supported in your treatment of this outcome: Diagnose proxy, load-balancer, NAT, connection-pool, and slow-reader behavior with capacity, ownership, and cost evidence.

Where does your evidence stop transferring to production for this outcome, and how is that boundary disclosed: Compare HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 through setup, multiplexing, stream isolation, fallback, observability, and client-network constraints.

What dissent should a skeptical reviewer raise about your treatment of this outcome, and what follow-up evidence would resolve it: Diagnose nine hidden network faults from preserved evidence before reveal and design reruns that separate credible causes.

What changed belief or reversal condition follows from your work on this outcome, and where is it recorded: Defend a protocol and topology decision through client outcomes, security, cost, ownership, migration, rollback, and reversal conditions.
